note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting with worsening wheeze and breathlessness since yesterday, associated with a viral upper respiratory infection.
The patient has a history of using salbutamol twice a day.
The patient is prescribed Clenil (beclometasone) 100 micrograms, two puffs twice daily, but adherence is poor.
The patient reports a tight chest and a small amount of clear sputum.
The patient had a feverish episode two days ago.
The patient has one previous hospital admission three years ago for two nights.
The patient has never required intensive care or a breathing tube.
The patient uses an e-cigarette daily.
The patient's vital signs include a breathing rate of 24, heart rate of 108, and oxygen saturation of 95% on air.
The examination reveals widespread bilateral wheeze with good air entry.
The patient's peak expiratory flow (PEF) is 250 L/min, which is 55% of their best.
Following a 5 mg nebulised salbutamol dose, the patient's PEF improved to 380 L/min (84% of best), breathing rate decreased to 18, and oxygen saturation increased to 98%.
The patient has a moderate acute asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral infection.
The patient showed a good response to the bronchodilator.
The patient has poor preventer adherence.
The plan includes prescribing prednisolone 40 mg once daily for five days.
The plan includes an inhaler technique check before discharge.
Discharge is planned if the patient remains stable after one hour of observation.
The patient is scheduled for a GP or asthma nurse review within two working days for inhaler review and asthma action plan.
Safety netting advice includes calling 999 if the patient needs their blue inhaler more often than every four hours, is too breathless to speak, or has blue lips.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician observed the patient is 'a bit wheezy'.
Patient reports having a cold for a few days and asthma worsening since yesterday.
Patient has a history of using salbutamol twice a day.
Patient corrected their salbutamol usage: it has been every two hours, maybe more, since last night.
Patient is on Clenil (brown preventer) 100 micrograms, meant to be taken twice a day.
The dose of Clenil is 100 micrograms, two puffs.
Patient was previously hospitalized once about three years ago for two nights.
Patient has never required intensive care or a breathing tube.
Patient reports symptoms include a tight chest and a bit of clear phlegm.
Patient reports feeling 'a bit hot' a couple of days ago with the cold.
Patient does not smoke but vapes every day.
Patient has an allergy to Aspirin, which causes chest tightness, leading to a previous hospital visit.
Examination findings: Breathing rate is 24, heart rate is 108, oxygen levels are 95 percent on air.
Examination findings: Clinician can hear wheeze all over the chest, on both sides, but air is getting in everywhere.
Peak flow meter reading is 250 L/min.
Patient's best peak flow reading is about 450 L/min.
The patient has a moderate asthma attack.
Treatment plan: Give a nebuliser with salbutamol (5 mg) and start prednisolone (40 mg once daily for five days).
Post-treatment findings: Peak flow is now 380 L/min (84% of best), breathing rate is 18, and oxygen is 98 percent.
Discharge condition: Patient can go home if stable for the next hour.
Instruction: Patient must use the brown inhaler every day, even when feeling well.
Follow-up plan: Patient needs to see a GP or asthma nurse within two working days for inhaler review and asthma action plan.
Safety netting instruction: Call 999 if the patient needs their blue inhaler more than every four hours, is too breathless to speak, or has blue lips.
